newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Sumitomo lawsuits refiled under seal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Sumitomo lawsuits refiled under seal.

text.p: A clutch of lawsuits filed against Sumitomo Corp alleging that the Japanese trade house and others manipulated the copper market were rolled into one, beefed up with fresh evidence and refiled under seal at a New York court on Thursday, an attorney for the plaintiffs said.

Fresh information gathered from copper industry players in return for keeping their identity secrect from the public was included in the lawsuit, said Geoffrey Horn, an attorney with Lovell & Skirnick, the firm representing the plaintiffs.
The consolidated lawsuit was filed under seal at the Southern District of New York Federal Court. No dollar figure for damages has been included.
The fresh information comes from subpoenas produced under confidentiality orders and served against banks, warehouses, trading firms and non-profit organizations, Horn said. He declined to name them.
No futures exchanges were subpoenaed, Horn said.

Thursday's refiling consolidates lawsuits filed last year by individual investors Stephen Carney, Benjamin Westfried, and father and son Vincent and Eric Zuccarelli alleging that Sumitomo Corp, its disgraced former head copper trader, Yasuo Hamanaka, Global Minerals and Metals Corp and its president David Campbell, and U.S. operations of U.K. based Winchester Commodities rigged the red metal market.
Horn said additional defendants were included in Thursday's filing, but Birch Brokerage has been dropped.
Horn declined to name the new defendents or indicate what fresh information was included because the filing was under seal, for the judge's eyes only.
Some documents would be made public Friday, the law firm said.
Global and Winchester dismissed the original lawsuits.
Some brokers have also expressed skepticism about the likely success of such court cases.
Last year the FBI subpoenaed Global as part of the U.S. regulatory probe into the Sumitomo scandal.
Holding on to much of the copper stocks in the London Metal Exchange warehouse in Long Beach was a key tool in propping up metal prices, the consolidated lawsuit reiterated, Horn said.
In June last year Sumitomo stunned the metals world by announcing it lost $1.8 billion, later swelling to $2.6 billion, due to unauthorised copper dealings by Hamanaka.
Hamanaka has admitted fraud and forgery in a trial which continues in Tokyo, but Sumitomo has said there was no evidence of market rigging.
This has not deterred the U.S. plaintiffs with their price manipulation allegations.
"The Japanese authorities said there was no wrongdoing in their country except for fraud, and that's the way they are dealing with it," Horn said.
Although the consolidated lawsuit is a class action case, no class has been certified yet by the judge, but Horn said this will be done later.
